q-ai-01.right: Its type and approximate average depth
wrong: Its R-value and the year it was installed
Its chemical composition and fire rating
Its upgrade cost and the R-value to add

q-ai-02.right: Missing insulation there; recommend it be restored
wrong: A roof leak above that ceiling; refer to a roofer
A plumbing leak in the ceiling; call a plumber
Nothing, because NC excludes measuring R-values

q-ai-03.right: Report it: the fan must vent outdoors, not into the attic
wrong: Acceptable, because the attic itself is vented to outdoors
Acceptable as long as the duct run is insulated
Not reportable; exhaust fans are not in NC scope
q-ai-03.explain: NC requires inspecting bathroom venting systems. Moist air dumped into the attic condenses on cold sheathing, and attic vents cannot carry it off fast enough. The dark sheathing near this duct is often the result.

q-ai-04.right: Keep insulation off the soffit vents so eave air can flow
wrong: Stop wind-driven rain from entering through the soffits
Hold the insulation tight against the roof deck
Block birds and insects from nesting in the eaves
q-ai-04.explain: Baffles hold insulation back so air can flow from the eave to the ridge. Soffit intake plus ridge exhaust is a pair. Blocked intake means a ridge vent with nothing to pull.

q-ai-05.right: 1 sq ft per 150 sq ft, or 1 per 300 when conditions are met
wrong: 1 sq ft per 50 sq ft, or 1 per 100 with a ridge vent
1 sq ft per 1,500 sq ft, or 1 per 3,000 with soffits
1 sq ft per 300 sq ft, or 1 per 600 with a vapor retarder
q-ai-05.explain: The base ratio is 1 sq ft of net free vent area per 150 sq ft of attic floor. The 1/300 option applies with balanced high and low venting or a vapor retarder in some climates. Describe what you see; you are not required to calculate it.

q-ai-06.right: Where readily visible evidence indicates a problem
wrong: No; moving insulation is outside the inspection scope
In each attic, at several spots, to check the drywall
When the client asks and is present to watch

q-ai-07.right: A safety concern: recommend correction per the manufacturer
wrong: Acceptable if the ladder holds your full weight when you test it
Cosmetic, since the ladder still folds and unfolds
Not reportable, because attic stairs are excluded
q-ai-07.explain: The ladder may detach under load. Manufacturers specify fastener type and count, and drywall screws are brittle and snap under shear. Recommend correction per the manufacturer's installation instructions.

wrong: Each one in the house
Those in the bedrooms
One per floor of the house

q-ai-10.right: Acceptable; worn paint is cosmetic and excluded
wrong: Repair item; recommend sanding and repainting the edge
Monitor for structural movement around the frame
Refer to a carpenter to evaluate the door

q-ai-11.right: Where the duct ends, by following it in the attic
wrong: Nothing more; a fan that pulls air is working
The fan motor's amperage, using a clamp meter
The fan's noise rating, printed on the housing label

q-ai-12.right: Describe it and recommend finding the moisture source
wrong: Call it mold and recommend remediation by a mold specialist
Call it normal aging of the plywood sheathing
Call it a roof leak and recommend roof replacement
q-ai-12.explain: NC excludes determining mold, so describe the discoloration without naming it and recommend finding the moisture source and further evaluation. Eave discoloration often points to poor ventilation or exhaust ducts venting into the attic.

q-dk-01.right: Report it; nails are not an acceptable ledger connection
wrong: Acceptable if there are many nails at close spacing along it
Acceptable on smaller decks, under about 10 ft wide
Monitor it, unless the ledger is visibly pulling away
q-dk-01.explain: Ledgers need bolts or lag screws into the house framing. Nailed ledgers pulling away are a leading cause of deck collapse. Recommend evaluation and correction by a qualified contractor.

q-dk-02.right: Water would sit behind the ledger and rot the rim joist
wrong: To give the deck a finished look where it meets the siding
To keep termites and carpenter ants out of the ledger
To stop the ledger from swelling and expanding in heat
q-dk-02.explain: Water running down the wall would otherwise sit between the ledger and the house, rotting the rim joist the ledger hangs on. Flashing laps behind the siding and over the ledger, shingle-fashion, so water always lands outside.

q-dk-03.right: Veneer is not structural, so it cannot carry the ledger
wrong: Brick is acceptable as long as the through-bolts are galvanized
Bolts through brick hold better than lag screws in wood
It is a cosmetic concern, since the mortar may crack
q-dk-03.explain: Veneer is a cladding tied loosely to the wall. The ledger must bear on the house framing, or the deck should be freestanding. Under load the veneer can pull away with the deck attached.

q-dk-04.right: Report it: every hole needs the specified fasteners
wrong: Acceptable if most of the holes are filled with nails
Acceptable, because screws are stronger than nails
Cosmetic, as long as the hangers are not bent
q-dk-04.explain: Hangers need every hole filled with the manufacturer's specified fasteners. A hanger is only as strong as its fasteners, and drywall screws are brittle and snap under shear.

q-dk-06.right: Over 30 in above grade within 36 in horizontally
wrong: On each deck, whatever its height above the ground
Above 48 in, measured at the deck's outer edge
When the deck has stairs or is over 24 in high
q-dk-06.explain: A guard is required when the walking surface is more than 30 in above the grade below at any point within 36 in horizontally. The 36 in reach accounts for sloping ground beside the deck edge.

q-dk-08.right: So sleeves and bag straps cannot catch on an open end
wrong: To make the rail stiffer at the spot where people grab it
For appearance, so the rail looks finished at the end
To keep rainwater from soaking into the cut end grain

q-dk-09.right: Report decay at the post base and refer to a contractor
wrong: Acceptable, because ground-contact treated wood resists rot
Monitor it, since the deck is not visibly leaning
Not reportable, since probing is an invasive test
q-dk-09.explain: Refer to a qualified contractor. NC requires probing wood where deterioration is suspected, even though the inspection is otherwise non-invasive. A rotted post is a direct break in the load path.

q-rf-01.right: Report the methods used to inspect the roofing
wrong: Walk on the roofing when it is safe to do so
Inspect solar panels, antennas, and other accessories
Certify the roof's remaining life for insurance

q-rf-02.right: Water can run down the pipe into the attic
wrong: It is cosmetic until the rubber falls away
It restricts airflow through the plumbing vent
Boots are part of plumbing, not the roof
q-rf-02.explain: Water can run down the pipe through the crack into the attic, so recommend repair by a roofer. Pipe boots are a top leak source as rubber ages in sunlight. Check the sheathing below from the attic.

wrong: 1 in
12 in
3 ft
q-rf-03.explain: Higher in snow country, and about 7 ft where the roof is occupied, such as a roof deck. The 3 ft figure is the chimney rule, not the vent rule.

q-rf-04.right: Lets warm, moist attic air out at the highest point
wrong: Supplies combustion air to an attic furnace
Cools the shingles from below to slow their aging
Lets the roof deck expand along the ridge in heat
q-rf-04.explain: It is the exhaust, paired with intake at the soffits. Exhaust without intake does little. Inspect both ends of the air path.

q-rf-05.right: The underside of the sheathing, for leak stains
wrong: Shingle granule loss on the north-facing slopes
Gutter condition and the downspout slope
Chimney crown cracks and missing mortar caps
q-rf-05.explain: From the attic you check the underside of the sheathing for leak stains and condensation. NC lists signs of leaks or abnormal condensation on building components as part of the roofing inspection.

q-rf-06.right: Extend 3 ft above the landing, 1 ft out per 4 ft of height
wrong: Extend 1 ft above the landing, 1 ft out per 2 ft of rise
Rest against the gutter, 1 ft out per 4 ft of height
Stand upright against the wall, 3 ft above the eave

q-rf-07.right: Gutters, downspouts, leaders, and splash blocks
wrong: The roof covering, flashing, and the ridge vents
Gutters and the underground storm drain lines
Interior floor drains and the sump pump pit
q-rf-07.explain: Gutters, downspouts, leaders, splash blocks, and similar components. NC requires these to be inspected with the roof. Their job is to carry water off the roof and away from the building.

q-rf-08.right: Skylights, chimneys, and other roof penetrations
wrong: Antennae, satellite dishes, and their roof mounts
Lightning arrestors and their ground wiring
De-icing cables along the eaves and gutters

q-ra-01.right: Protect the asphalt from UV and add fire resistance
wrong: Bond the shingles together into one sealed layer
Seal around the nail holes when the sun warms them
Make the shingle waterproof, so underlayment is optional
q-ra-01.explain: They protect the asphalt from sunlight (UV) and add fire and impact resistance. Once granules wash away, UV breaks down the asphalt fast. Heavy loss and granules in the gutters signal an ageing roof.

q-ra-02.right: Each exposed nail is a leak path into the deck
wrong: They are cosmetic once the heads have rusted
They matter in hurricane zones, not in normal weather
Exposed nails are normal along the ridge and hips
q-ra-02.explain: Correct nails are hidden under the next course. Water follows the nail shank into the deck. Recommend sealing or correction by a roofer.

q-ra-03.right: Where the next course covers them, on the nailing line
wrong: Through the exposed tab, so the wind will not lift it
Above the nailing line, near the top edge of the shingle
On the exposed tab, as long as each head is sealed
q-ra-03.explain: Place them on the manufacturer's nailing line, below the edge of the overlying course, so the next shingle covers them. Nails too high miss the shingle below and reduce wind resistance; nails too low are exposed. High-wind areas call for at least six per shingle.

q-ra-04.right: Carries water into the gutter and protects the deck edge
wrong: Supports the gutter and keeps it pitched toward the downspout
Decorative trim that hides the cut edge of the deck
Vents the attic at the eave, like a soffit strip
q-ra-04.explain: It carries water off the roof edge into the gutter and protects the edge of the deck and fascia. Without it, water wicks back under the shingles and rots the deck edge and fascia.

q-ra-05.right: One plane's shingles cross it; the other's are cut along it
wrong: Shingles from both planes are woven together through the valley
An open metal channel is left exposed, with shingles cut back
Shingles meet at the center line with no underlayment below
q-ra-05.explain: Shingles from one roof plane run across the valley, and the other plane's shingles are cut along the valley line. Closed-cut is a common and acceptable method. Know it so you do not call it a defect.

wrong: 1:12, with double underlayment below 3:12
3:12, with double underlayment above 6:12
4:12, with double underlayment from 4:12 to 6:12

q-ra-07.right: 24 in inside the exterior wall line
wrong: 6 in past the outer edge of the gutter
12 in up the roof from the drip edge
36 in up the slope from the eave edge

q-ra-08.right: Model code does not allow a re-cover over two layers
wrong: A third layer is fine if longer nails reach the deck
Re-covering is better, since the old layers add insulation
Layer count does not matter for asphalt shingles
q-ra-08.explain: Model code does not allow a re-cover over two existing layers, and a tear-off also lets the roofer inspect the sheathing. Extra layers add weight and hide deck damage. The 25 Standards course recommends removing the old shingles.

q-fd-01.right: Differential settlement of part of the wall
wrong: Normal shrinkage of the mortar as it cures
Lateral soil pressure pushing the wall inward
Freeze-thaw damage to the block faces and joints
q-fd-01.explain: Part of the wall has moved down relative to the rest. Report the pattern, width, and any displacement, and refer to a structural engineer if it is wide or offset.

q-fd-02.right: Soil pressure is overcoming the wall; refer to an engineer
wrong: It is typical shrinkage of block walls as mortar cures
It comes from the house settling evenly on its footings
It is cosmetic once it has been painted and sealed
q-fd-02.explain: It indicates lateral soil pressure overcoming the wall; refer to a structural engineer. Block walls resist sideways pressure poorly. Bowing means the wall is moving, not just cracking.

q-fd-03.right: Efflorescence: salts left by water; a moisture sign
wrong: Mold growth on the block; recommend professional remediation
Early structural failure of the block faces
Termite mud tubes; refer to a pest control company
q-fd-03.explain: Efflorescence is salt left behind as water moves through masonry. It is evidence of moisture, not structural damage by itself. Look for the water source, but do not over-call the deposit itself.

q-fd-04.right: Report it and refer to a structural engineer
wrong: Acceptable, since masonry piers crack as they age
Patch it with mortar and note it as repaired
Monitor it, since the pier is not leaning

q-fd-05.right: Report inadequate bearing under the girder
wrong: Acceptable; stacked shims are a normal way to level it
Cosmetic, as long as the floor above feels level
Not reportable without first calculating the load
q-fd-05.explain: The girder needs full, solid bearing on the pier. Crushed or loose shims let the floor settle and concentrate the load on a small area.

q-fd-06.right: 6 ft apart, with one within 12 in of each plate end
wrong: 10 ft apart, with one within 36 in of each end
4 ft apart, with two bolts at each plate end
8 ft apart, with one at the center of each plate

q-fd-07.right: The type of each structural system, foundation to roof
wrong: The depth and width of the footings below grade
The compressive strength of the foundation concrete
The soil type and its bearing capacity below the footings
q-fd-07.explain: NC lists the type of foundation, floor structure, wall structure, columns or piers, ceiling structure, and roof structure. For this house: block foundation walls and masonry piers over a vented crawlspace. Describing type is required; measuring strength is excluded.

q-fd-08.right: Describe the lean, explain it, and refer to an engineer
wrong: Calculate the load on the pier to judge its adequacy
Specify the repair method so the seller can get bids
Estimate the cost of a new pier for negotiations
q-fd-08.explain: Describe the lean and its implications, and refer to a structural engineer. NC excludes calculating strength or adequacy and reporting methods or costs of correction. You report, explain, and refer.

q-rt-01.right: From a ladder or the ground, without walking on the tiles
wrong: Walk on the tiles near the center of each slope
Walk on the tiles along the ridge, where they are strong
Lift a few tiles to see the condition of the underlayment
q-rt-01.explain: Inspect from a ladder, the ground, or another vantage point, and report the method. Clay tile breaks under foot, and you would own the damage. NC does not require walking any roof.

q-rt-02.right: The underlayment below will deteriorate in sun and water
wrong: It is cosmetic, since tile is mostly there for looks
Cracked tile still sheds water; replace it at resale
It matters on new roofs still under warranty, not older ones
q-rt-02.explain: Tile is the armour; the underlayment is the waterproofing. A broken tile leaves the underlayment exposed to sun and water. Refer to a roofer experienced with tile.

q-rt-03.right: Fastener or hanging failure; loose tiles can fall
wrong: Normal thermal movement of the tiles in summer heat
The roof slope is too steep to hold tile in place
An installation laid too tight, pushing tiles out
q-rt-03.explain: The gap exposes the underlayment. Slipped tiles are both a leak and a falling-object hazard over a walkway. Refer for repair.

q-rt-04.right: The underlayment, which is the real water barrier
wrong: The tiles themselves, which are fully waterproof
The mortar packed between the tiles at the laps
The glaze or sealer coating on the tile surface
q-rt-04.explain: The tile sheds most water, but the underlayment is the real water barrier. This is why old tile roofs often need re-underlayment while the tiles themselves are reusable.

wrong: 2:12; double underlayment up to 4:12
1-1/2:12; double underlayment up to 3:12
3-1/2:12; double underlayment up to 6:12
q-rt-05.explain: The minimum is 2-1/2:12, with double underlayment from 2-1/2:12 to 4:12. Like shingles, tile sheds water by lapping, and low slopes need extra underlayment. The 2:12 figure is the asphalt shingle rule.

wrong: Major defect; mortar fails over time
Repair item; recommend repointing
Monitor and re-inspect yearly

q-rt-07.right: Excluded; inspect it only if the written contract adds it
wrong: It is in scope and inspected the same as the main house
It may not be inspected, even if the client asks
Its electrical and roof are inspected, nothing else
q-rt-07.explain: NC .1107(c)(8) excludes detached buildings. A contract can expand scope, and once you inspect it, the report must cover it properly.

q-rt-08.right: Tile is far heavier; have an engineer check the framing
wrong: A roof that holds shingles will hold tile as well
The underlayment needs upgrading, but not the framing
Tile is lighter than asphalt, so framing is fine
q-rt-08.explain: Tile is several times heavier than asphalt, so the framing must be evaluated by an engineer before conversion. Converting adds a large dead load the original framing may not have been designed for.

wrong: Bedrooms on upper floors, not the ground floor
Each habitable room, including the kitchen
The primary bedroom and the basement

q-eg-03.right: 9 sq ft, with 36 in of projection and width
wrong: 4 sq ft, with 24 in of projection and width
10 sq ft, with 42 in of projection and width
7 sq ft, with 32 in of projection and width

q-eg-04.right: A safety hazard: the bars need an inside release
wrong: Acceptable, since the bars improve the bedroom's security
Cosmetic, as long as the bars are painted and sound
Acceptable if the bedroom door leads to two exits
q-eg-04.explain: Bars on an escape window must release from inside without a key, tool, or special knowledge. In a fire the window may be the only way out, and in the dark and smoke nobody can find a key.

q-eg-05.right: Report the bars; recommend confirming the release works
wrong: Mark them acceptable, since a release lever is present
Operate the release yourself, using force if needed, to be sure
Report them as a code violation and recommend removal
q-eg-05.explain: Report the bars, note the release, and recommend confirming that it works easily from inside. Not required to operate means you describe, explain the stakes, and recommend verification.

q-eg-07.right: A door from the garage straight into a sleeping room
wrong: A door from the garage into an inside hallway
A solid 1-3/8 in door from the garage into the kitchen
An overhead door with photo-eyes and an auto-reverse

q-eg-08.right: 32 in of clear width and 78 in of height
wrong: 28 in of clear width and 72 in of height
36 in of clear width and 84 in of height
30 in of clear width and 80 in of height

q-pl-01.right: It can siphon its own water seal and let in sewer gas
wrong: It drains too slowly and clogs more than a P-trap
It is a dated style choice with no real effect
It wastes water each time the fixture is used

q-pl-03.right: No; NC does not require operating stop valves
wrong: Yes, cycle each stop to prove it shuts off
Yes, but just the hot side, where scale builds up
Yes, if the client asks you to check them
q-pl-03.explain: NC .1109(d)(5) does not require operating valves other than flush valves, fixture faucets, and hose faucets, and old stops can leak once turned. Report visible corrosion or leaks at the stops instead.

q-pl-04.right: The ridges trap debris, and it is not an approved drain
wrong: It is the modern standard, replacing rigid PVC drain pipe
It is acceptable if the run is short and well sloped
It matters at bathroom sinks, not at the kitchen sink
q-pl-04.explain: The ridges trap debris and clog easily, and it is not an approved trap or drain material; recommend smooth-wall pipe. Corrugated flex drains sag, collect grease, and can let the trap seal fail.

q-pl-05.right: Report the active leak and refer to a plumber
wrong: Acceptable, since drain joints drip now and then
Not reportable, because the crawlspace is excluded
Monitor it and re-check at the final walkthrough
q-pl-05.explain: Check the wood below with the moisture meter. A leak in the crawlspace runs unseen for years. Follow it to the framing.

q-pl-06.right: Describe it as PEX supply; acceptable as installed
wrong: Report it as polybutylene, a known failure-prone pipe
Report it as a defect, since plastic supply is not allowed
Recommend replacing it with galvanized steel piping

q-pl-08.right: A loose toilet; the wax seal may be broken
wrong: Acceptable, since toilets can rock a little
Cosmetic, once the caulk at the base is redone
Tighten the flange bolts yourself and move on
q-pl-08.explain: Refer to a plumber and check the subfloor. Movement breaks the seal, allowing hidden leaks and sewer gas. InterNACHI lists loose toilets as reportable.

q-pl-09.right: Usable flow at the top fixture while another runs
wrong: A flow rate of at least 5 gallons per minute at the main
Steady flow at the kitchen faucet with nothing else on
Static water pressure above 40 psi at the hose bib
q-pl-09.explain: Functional flow is a usable flow at the highest fixture in the dwelling while another fixture is operated at the same time. NC defines it by use, not by measurement. Run the top-floor shower and flush a toilet at the same time.

q-pl-11.right: The piping materials and the main shutoff location
wrong: Whether the water supply is public or a private well
The water quality from the well, by test kit
Whether a backflow device is present at the main
q-pl-11.explain: You describe the supply and distribution piping materials and the location of any main shutoff. NC excludes deciding public versus private supply, well water quality, and backflow devices.

q-pl-12.right: To let air in so draining water does not siphon traps
wrong: To let rainwater in to flush the drain lines
To cool the drain pipes when hot water is draining
To raise water pressure at the upper fixtures
q-pl-12.explain: Vents let air into the drain so flowing water does not siphon the trap seals, and they carry sewer gas above the roof. This is the prerequisite for every trap question. No air in, and the falling water pulls the trap seal out behind it.

q-st-01.right: Report it and refer to a structural engineer
wrong: Acceptable if the cut is small and near the end
Acceptable if the ceiling below has no cracks
Repair it by nailing a scrap board over the cut
q-st-01.explain: Engineered trusses cannot be cut without an engineer's repair design. Every truss member is designed for a specific load. A cut web can redistribute forces in ways nobody calculated.

wrong: One-half of the joist depth (D/2)
One-third of the joist depth (D/3)
One-quarter of the joist depth (D/4)
q-st-02.explain: No notches in the middle third, and no more than D/4 at the ends; D/4 is the end rule, not the outer-third rule. Engineered joists cannot be notched without the engineer.

q-st-03.right: No larger than D/3, at least 2 in from each edge
wrong: No larger than D/2, close to the top or bottom edge
No larger than D/6, at least 2 in from each edge
As large as needed, as long as it is centered
q-st-03.explain: No larger than one-third of the joist depth (D/3), and at least 2 in from the top and bottom edges. D/6 is the notch rule, not the hole rule. Holes near the edges cut the fibers carrying the most stress. Keep them centered and modest.

q-st-04.right: Typical, not a structural defect; note it for monitoring
wrong: Structural movement; refer to an engineer to evaluate
Foundation failure; recommend underpinning the piers
Moisture damage; refer to a roofer to find the leak
q-st-04.explain: Door and window corners concentrate stress, so hairline cracks there are common and NC treats cosmetic damage as excluded. It becomes a finding if it widens, offsets, or doors begin to bind; width, offset, binding doors, and sloped floors are what turn a crack into a movement finding.

q-st-05.right: Dead load is the building's own weight; live load varies
wrong: Dead load is snow on the roof; live load is the wind
Dead load is what a failed member carries; live, a sound one
They are two names for the same total design load
q-st-05.explain: Dead load is the weight of the building itself; live load is variable, such as people, furniture, and snow. A structural component, by NC definition, supports both. Every structural finding is about one of these loads losing its path.

q-st-06.right: Joists to girder to piers to footings to soil
wrong: Joists to trusses to walls to footings to soil
Girder to joists to piers to footings to soil
Joists to piers to girder to footings to soil
q-st-06.explain: Floor joists bear on the girder, the girder on the piers, the piers on the footings, and the footings on the soil. Tracing the load path is the prerequisite for judging any structural defect: find which link is weak.

q-st-07.right: Truss uplift: the drier bottom chord bows up in winter
wrong: Foundation settlement under the interior wall each winter
Seasonal shrinkage of the drywall tape at the wall corner
Roof leaks soaking and sagging the ceiling drywall
q-st-07.explain: The bottom chord, buried in insulation, stays warmer and drier than the top chords, so the truss bows upward seasonally. Uplift is common and usually not structural. Describe it, explain the seasonal pattern, and avoid over-calling.

q-st-08.right: Wood touching or near soil, and cut or notched framing
wrong: The adequacy of the foundation anchor bolting
The load capacity of each floor joist and girder
The engineering design of the roof truss system
q-st-08.explain: SOP 3.3 asks you to report wood in contact with or near soil, and cutting, notching, or boring of framing that may be a structural or safety concern. It asks for observed conditions, not engineering judgments on adequacy.
